title: Maxwell's Demon and the Physical Cost of Information
question: Can a being that merely sorts molecules by knowing their speeds break the second law of thermodynamics, and what does the answer reveal about information?
summary: A century-long puzzle about a molecule-sorting demon was resolved by showing that erasing information has an irreducible energy cost, revealing that information is physical and linking thermodynamics, computation, and life.
content:
A Thought Experiment That Wouldn't Die

In 1867, James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny being guarding a trapdoor between two chambers of gas. Whenever a fast molecule approached from the left, the demon opened the door; whenever a slow one approached from the right, it did the same. Over time, the right chamber grew hot and the left grew cold, all without any apparent expenditure of work. The second law of thermodynamics, which says entropy in an isolated system never decreases, seemed to have been broken by nothing more than attention.

The puzzle survived for more than a century because it is not really about gas. It asks whether knowing something about a system is a physical act with physical costs, or whether information floats free of the world it describes.

The First Answers: Measurement Has a Price

In 1929 Leo Szilard reduced the demon to its bare bones: a single molecule in a box. If you know which half the molecule occupies, you can insert a partition and let the molecule push a piston, extracting kT ln 2 of work. Szilard concluded that the act of measurement must generate at least that much entropy to save the second law. Later, Leon Brillouin argued that seeing a molecule requires bouncing light off it, and the photon carries away the needed entropy.

These answers felt plausible but turned out to be incomplete. Charles Bennett showed in the 1980s that measurement can, in principle, be done reversibly, with arbitrarily little dissipation. The demon could look for free. So where does the bill come due?

Landauer's Principle: Forgetting Is Expensive

The resolution came from Rolf Landauer, who in 1961 argued that erasing one bit of information must dissipate at least kT ln 2 of heat into the environment. Bennett realized this closes the loophole. The demon must record each molecule's speed to decide whether to open the door. Its memory is finite, so eventually it must erase old records to make room for new ones. That erasure produces exactly the entropy the demon seemed to destroy.

The lesson is striking: logically irreversible operations, those that map many possible inputs to one output, have an unavoidable thermodynamic cost. Information is not an abstraction hovering above physics; it is encoded in physical states, and manipulating it obeys physical law. In 2012 experimenters in Lyon measured the heat released when erasing a single bit stored in a colloidal particle and found it approached Landauer's bound.

Why It Matters Beyond the Box

Landauer's principle sets a floor beneath computation. Modern chips dissipate millions of times more energy per operation than the limit, but as transistors shrink, the bound becomes a horizon engineers can see. It also motivates reversible computing, in which no information is destroyed and, in principle, computation could approach zero dissipation.

The demon also reframes life itself. Cells behave like demons: molecular motors, ion pumps, and kinetic proofreading all use information about their surroundings to create local order, paying for it by consuming free energy. Erwin Schrodinger's idea that organisms feed on "negative entropy" becomes precise in this light. And in black hole physics, the question of whether information is destroyed when matter falls in is, at its core, a descendant of Maxwell's question.

The Deeper Puzzle

If entropy depends on what an observer knows, is it an objective property of a system or a measure of our ignorance? Physicists still disagree. Some treat thermodynamic entropy as fundamentally informational; others insist it is a property of physical states independent of any knower. The demon, it turns out, was never defeated so much as recruited, becoming the clearest bridge we have between physics and information.

perspectives.title: Thermodynamic Perspective
perspectives.description: The second law survives because the demon's memory must eventually be erased, and erasure dumps at least kT ln 2 of heat per bit into the environment.

perspectives.title: Computer Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Landauer's bound sets a fundamental floor on the energy cost of irreversible computation and motivates reversible logic as a path to ultra-efficient machines.

perspectives.title: Biological Perspective
perspectives.description: Living cells act as real Maxwell's demons, using information about their environment to build order, paid for with chemical free energy.

perspectives.title: Philosophical Perspective
perspectives.description: If entropy depends on what an observer knows, the demon forces us to ask whether entropy is objective or a measure of ignorance.

openQuestions: Is thermodynamic entropy fundamentally the same thing as information-theoretic entropy, or only mathematically analogous?
How close can practical computers get to the Landauer limit, and would reversible computing ever be worth its overhead?
How do quantum measurement and entanglement change the accounting of a quantum Maxwell's demon?
Does the observer-dependence of entropy imply the arrow of time is partly a feature of how we know the world?
